source: Tolman (1948) Cognitive maps in rats and men
finding: Tolman argued learning builds a map-like set in the nervous system, not stimulus-response links. The brain is a 'map control room', not a telephone exchange. Maps can be narrow (strip) or broad (comprehensive).
numbers: Theory paper. No single N. Cites five experiment families: latent learning, vicarious trial and error, searching for the stimulus, hypotheses, spatial orientation.
quote: the narrower and more strip-like the original map, the less will it carry over successfully to the new problem
limits: Strip map: one path from start to goal, fails when the route changes. Comprehensive map: wide arc of the environment, survives a new start or a blocked route. The test of map type is behaviour after a change.
agent_relevance: A schema state S2 should hold a broad map (states plus moves), not one stored route. The test is whether the agent copes when a move is blocked or the goal moves.

source: Blodgett (1929) latent learning in a six-unit alley maze, as reported in Tolman (1948)
finding: Rats given no food in the maze made many errors and seemed to learn little. Once food appeared, error curves dropped sharply on the following days. So they had learned the maze without reward.
numbers: Three groups: control fed daily; Group II first fed on day 7; Group III first fed on day 3. Exact error counts are only in figures, not read.
quote: They had been building up a 'map,' and could utilize the latter as soon as they were motivated
limits: Second-hand account. Tolman interprets the result in anthropomorphic terms; the source gives no statistics. A motivation account is not ruled out in the text read.
agent_relevance: Knowledge can be built without reward and used when the goal appears. Agent analogue: explore and record the task structure before any answer is scored.

source: Tolman and Honzik replication of Blodgett in a 14-unit T-maze, as reported in Tolman (1948)
finding: Repeated with larger groups and a 14-unit maze. The group first rewarded on day 11 (HNR-R) showed the same sudden drop in errors.
numbers: Three groups: never rewarded (HNR), always rewarded (HR), rewarded from day 11 (HNR-R). Numbers are in Fig. 6 of the paper, not in the text.
limits: No statistics in the text. Same lab tradition as the original.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Blodgett. Shows the effect is not a one-off.

source: Spence and Lippitt (reported in Tolman 1948): Y-maze latent learning with satiated rats
finding: Rats trained neither hungry nor thirsty, with food at the left arm and water at the right. Later made hungry or thirsty, they went to the arm holding the needed goal on the first trial, more often than chance.
numbers: Four trials a day for seven days, two left and two right. Test: hungry vs thirsty subgroup, first trial only. Tolman says 'statistically more frequently' with no counts.
quote: they had acquired a cognitive map to the effect that food was to the left and water to the right
limits: Only an abstract was published then; Tolman used a preliminary manuscript. Counts unknown.
agent_relevance: Strongest classical case that the map stores goal-location links apart from current drive. Agent analogue: store what is where, then pick the goal later.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning, Study I
finding: Humans learned a 3-phase task, then reward or transition values changed. People adjusted to both changes. Reward revaluation was easier than transition revaluation. Pure model-free and pure successor-representation (SR) models failed; a hybrid SR plus model-based mix fit best.
numbers: N=58 analysed of 69. Revaluation score: reward 0.520 (SEM 0.020), transition 0.450 (0.023), control 0.031. Reward vs transition t(57)=2.89, p<0.01. Transition vs control t(57)=9.05, p<0.001. Slower RT for transition, t(57)=2.08, p<0.05.
limits: Hybrid is a linear mixture 'for simplicity'. Model comparison shown in figures, no likelihoods reported. 11 excluded. Model-free not formally fit. Reward revaluation only about 52 percent of ceiling.
agent_relevance: Humans do not hold a full map or a cached value alone. A cheap predictive map plus on-demand planning matches them. Agent analogue: cached summary plus fresh search when a transition changes.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) Study II, active sequential task
finding: Second sample with one test trial per condition. Switching to the new best first action was most common after a reward change and lower after transition and policy changes.
numbers: N=88 analysed of 112 (24 excluded, 21 percent). Proportion switching: reward 0.659, transition 0.466, policy 0.500, control 0.080. Reward vs transition Wald Z=-2.85, p=.0034. Reward vs policy Z=-2.61, p=.0043. Policy vs transition p=.577.
limits: One binary trial per person per condition. The null for policy vs transition is absence of evidence. Dyna-style replay variants not tested.
agent_relevance: Even humans fail to update about a third to a half of the time after a structure change. A scaffold that rebuilds the map after a change beats trusting cached beliefs.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based reinforcement learning to model-free mechanisms
finding: Grid-world simulations (10x10, 100 states) compare cached-value TD, successor representation learned by TD (SR-TD), SR with replay (SR-Dyna), and full model-based planning. SR-TD passes latent learning but fails detour and policy revaluation. SR-Dyna passes all three if replay is large enough.
numbers: Latent learning (reward change): SR-TD, SR-MB, SR-Dyna, full MB pass; depth-limited model-free fails. Detour (transition change): SR-TD fails; SR-Dyna passes with enough replay. Policy revaluation: SR-TD and SR-MB fail; SR-Dyna passes. Policy simulation used 10,000 replay samples. Results are pass or fail, no rates.
quote: SR-TD cannot adjust its valuations to local changes in the transitions without first updating M
limits: Only the first half of the paper was read (the fetch covered 100,000 of 200,656 characters). Replay count k not found. Without enough replay SR-Dyna behaves like SR-TD. Grid-world only.
agent_relevance: Tolman's tests map to three changes: reward moved, path blocked, policy changed. A map with no replay or re-planning step fails the last two. Supports an S2 map plus an explicit re-plan operator.

source: Constantinescu, O'Reilly, Behrens (2016) Organizing conceptual knowledge in humans with a gridlike code, Science
finding: fMRI showed a six-fold (hexagonal) signal as people imagined bird shapes changing in an abstract 2D space (neck and leg length). Peaks appeared in entorhinal cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, the signature of grid cells, here for non-spatial concepts.
numbers: N=28 (2-4 sessions). Outcome accuracy 72.8 +/- 1.0 percent. Entorhinal peak Z=4.41; vmPFC Z=4.09; retrosplenial Z=4.73. Effect only at 6-fold: controls at 4, 5, 7, 8-fold p>0.15 within day. vmPFC hexagonal strength vs performance r=0.43, p=0.039. Cross-day vmPFC consistency t(20)=3.65, p<0.01.
quote: Non-spatial conceptual knowledge can be organized using a grid-like code in the human brain.
limits: Indirect fMRI signature, not single cells. Authors note the quadrature test may overestimate Z. None of 28 saw it as a map. Boundary: the signal weakens in old age (a09).
agent_relevance: Most direct evidence that the same machinery codes abstract task spaces. Supports building S2 as a 2D map of task features, not only a list.

source: Stangl, Achtzehn, Huber, Dietrich, Tempelmann, Wolbers (2018) Compromised grid-cell-like representations in old age, Curr Biol
finding: Replicates the hexadirectional entorhinal signal in young adults during virtual navigation and shows it is absent in older adults, who also path-integrate worse. A boundary condition on the grid-like signal.
numbers: Young adults: 6-fold t(19)=3.71, p=0.002; 5-fold p=0.983; 7-fold p=0.822. Older adults: 6-fold t(20)=-0.79, p=0.438. Young vs old t(39)=-2.66, p=0.011.
limits: Spatial task, not abstract. Small groups (20 and 21). Authors say the age effect is mostly instability over time.
agent_relevance: The signal is fragile and depends on a stable representation. Map quality varies and should be checked, not assumed.

source: Garvert, Dolan, Behrens (2017) A map of abstract relational knowledge in the human hippocampal-entorhinal cortex, eLife
finding: People saw object sequences from a random walk on a hidden graph. Next day, hippocampal-entorhinal fMRI adaptation tracked graph distance. Distance was best explained by 'communicability' (a sum over future states), close to the successor representation, not by Euclidean or link distance.
numbers: 23 participants in the fMRI experiment. Response times: communicability t(25)=2.77, p=0.01; link distance t=-0.40, p=0.69; Euclidean t=-0.85, p=0.40 (taken from the authors' reply text in the page).
limits: Reviewers raised missing behavioural data and use of a peak voxel from a spatial study. Small N. Implicit learning, no explicit planning.
agent_relevance: A map built from experience stores predictive closeness, so 'near' means 'likely reachable soon'. Agent analogue: rank next moves by reachability, not surface similarity.

source: Aronov, Nevers, Tank (2017) Mapping of a non-spatial dimension by the hippocampal-entorhinal circuit, Nature
finding: Rats moved a joystick to raise a sound along a frequency axis. CA1 and medial entorhinal neurons formed discrete firing fields at particular frequencies. Place and grid cells took part.
numbers: N=9 rats behaviour (release in target zone 70.8 +/- 2.6 percent of trials); 2208 CA1 units (5 rats) and 1164 MEC units (9 rats). 40.0 percent of CA1 and 51.3 percent of MEC cells task-modulated (p<0.01). Of 295 place cells 25.1 percent task-modulated; of 105 grid cells 34.3 percent. Non-place CA1 cells 34.7 percent, non-grid MEC cells 46.5 percent.
limits: Place and grid cells were somewhat less likely to join than other cells. One-dimensional variable. Spatial confounds (head movement) needed apparatus changes.
agent_relevance: First single-cell evidence that non-spatial dimensions get place-like fields, supporting the claim in the subfield row.

source: Park, Miller, Nili, Ranganath, Boorman (2020) Map making: constructing, combining, and inferring on abstract cognitive maps, Neuron
finding: People learned two 4x4 social hierarchies from pairwise comparisons, then linked them through one hub. They inferred never-seen comparisons, with 2D distance signals in entorhinal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
numbers: N=27 analysed of 33 scanned (282 started training, 82 passed day 2). Inference accuracy 93.6 +/- 0.77 percent. RT faster with 2D Euclidean distance. Bayesian exceedance probability 0.82 to 0.91 in EC and vmPFC. Hippocampus: no univariate effect.
limits: Heavy attrition and strict inclusion; some effects missed the strictest correction; no hexadirectional test; signal could reflect decision certainty; young students only. Read from the first 100,000 of 182,365 characters.
agent_relevance: Humans can join two partial maps through a shared hub and infer new links. Agent analogue: when a subproblem shares an anchor with a solved one, join the maps.

source: Whittington, Muller, Mark, Chen, Barry, Burgess, Behrens (2020) The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine, Cell
finding: A neural network that predicts the next observation on graph walks learns grid-like entorhinal codes for structure and place-like hippocampal codes that bind structure to sensory items. It transfers structure to new objects, solving family-tree and transitive tasks.
numbers: Task: predict next observation on graph walks. Example: after 'Bob is the brother of Cat who is Fran's mother', TEM answers 'Fran' to 'who is Bob's niece?'. Place-grid correlation r_data 0.27-0.32 vs r_model 0.31. Family tree used 10 relation types.
quote: TEM returns B to the query what is 3 more than E
limits: Not a reinforcement-learning agent; actions are given. Sensory observations are random so structure is the only cause. Fit to data is qualitative for many cell types.
agent_relevance: Core separation: reusable structure (the map) vs item content. Matches the S2 idea of a task-structure slot reused across tasks with different contents.

source: Whittington, Warren, Behrens (2022) Relating transformers to models and neural representations of the hippocampal formation, ICLR
finding: A transformer with recurrent position encodings (TEM-t) reproduces place and grid cells and learns the TEM tasks faster than TEM. Self-attention is mathematically close to the TEM memory retrieval step.
numbers: TEM-t is more sample-efficient and faster than TEM; the paper says TEM training takes much longer and they stopped TEM at 20,000 steps. Exact ratios not extracted (garbled layout).
limits: The authors say the comparison is not fully fair (code and tuning differ). Only spatial and TEM tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled reason to expect transformers, and so LLMs, to carry map-like state in context, but only with the right position code.

source: Li, Hopkins, Bau, Viegas, Pfister, Wattenberg (2023) Emergent world representations: a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello-GPT), ICLR
finding: A GPT trained only on Othello move sequences predicts legal moves almost perfectly and holds an internal board state. Nonlinear probes read it out and changing it changes the next-move output.
numbers: Illegal move rate 0.01 percent (synthetic) and 5.17 percent (championship); untrained 93.29 percent. Linear probe error never below 20 percent. Nonlinear probe error low as 1.7 percent at a late layer for synthetic. Intervention errors 0.12 (natural) and 0.06 (unnatural) vs null baseline 2.68 and 2.59, 1000 cases each.
limits: Toy game with deterministic rules. Linear probes failed here; later work (Nanda 2023, not opened) is reported by Gurnee and Tegmark to find a linear form. Not shown for natural-language tasks.
agent_relevance: Next-token training can yield a causal internal map of a rule-governed space. But it is a trained model, not a scaffolded one.

source: Ivanitskiy et al. (2023) Structured world representations in maze-solving transformers
finding: Small transformers trained on mazes build a maze map: one token's residual stream can be linearly decoded to the whole maze. Specific 'adjacency heads' find valid next steps.
numbers: Best model (jirpy) on out-of-distribution pRDFS mazes: 70.7 percent exactly correct, 87.1 percent valid, 100 percent reach target. Hallway model: 24.2 percent exactly correct. Linear probes above 90 percent accuracy in best models at layer 2; poor performers never above 80 percent.
limits: Tiny models trained on mazes, not general LLMs. Link between map quality and performance is correlational here.
agent_relevance: Better performers have a cleaner map. Suggests checking that the agent's written map is accurate before trusting the plan built on it.

source: Gurnee and Tegmark (2023) Language models represent space and time, ICLR 2024
finding: Linear probes on Llama-2 activations decode world, US and NYC coordinates and historical dates. Space and time are linearly represented, with 'space neurons' and 'time neurons'.
numbers: Out-of-sample R^2 at 60 percent depth, Llama-2-70b linear: World 0.896, USA 0.825, NYC 0.237, historical 0.804, entertainment 0.806, headlines 0.645. Largest model row: World 0.911, NYC 0.359. Held-out blocks: World proximity error 0.071 nominal vs 0.170 held out (chance 0.5).
limits: Probes can learn the map themselves; held-out tests show relative but not absolute position generalises. Static facts, not planning. NYC is weakest.
agent_relevance: LLMs hold coarse maps of the world in their weights. This does not show they use a map when planning on a new graph.

source: Momennejad, Hu, Wang, Mao, Williams, Mohamed et al. (2023) Evaluating cognitive maps and planning in large language models with CogEval, arXiv 2309.15129
finding: Eight LLMs were tested on planning tasks built from human cognitive-map experiments (several graphs, three domains; path, detour, shortcut, reward and transition revaluation). They look competent on simple paths but fail on harder structures with invalid-edge hallucination and loops.
numbers: GPT-4-32k mean score (SD): 1-step path 0.99 (0.08), 2-step 0.82 (0.35), 3-step 0.55 (0.38), n-step 0.47 (0.38), policy revaluation 0.21 (0.18), reward revaluation 0.67 (0.40), transition revaluation 0.60 (0.42). Logistic regression: model chi2(11)=2357.87, graph chi2=3431.53, all p<.001; temperature chi2(11)=1.28, p=.53. 30 generations per condition.
limits: Early models (GPT-4, Claude-1, Bard, LLaMA-13B), 2023 snapshot. Preprint. Text-only prompts, no code tools. The table's second number may be SD or SE (labelled SE in the paper).
agent_relevance: The key LLM test of this subfield. Planning drops with path length and on policy change. Backs an external, code-held map with checks.

source: CogEval Experiment 2: graph-search hints (BFS, DFS) and chain of thought (Momennejad et al. 2023)
finding: Giving GPT-4 BFS or DFS instructions helped only a little and not consistently. On a community-graph shortest path one cluster away, GPT-4 success could not exceed 10 percent in 30 runs.
numbers: Cluster counting (graph D): BFS or DFS helped at some temperatures. Shortcut with CoT: GPT-4 scored 1.00 on non-teleporting shortcut but 0.50 on teleporting shortcut (SE 0.00 for both).
limits: One graph family. Few runs per temperature.
agent_relevance: Prompt hints do not give a map. Re-affirms G2 and G3: use code to hold the graph and check each move.

source: CogEval failure modes (Momennejad et al. 2023, discussion)
finding: When asked to list connected rooms (one step), LLMs do well. On community-structured graphs they hallucinate edges, give long trajectories instead of shortest paths, and loop.
numbers: One-step path near ceiling (GPT-4 0.99). Longer: 3-step 0.55; n-step 0.47. Small models (LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B) 0.04 to 0.06 on 3-step.
limits: Failure counts are not tabulated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Failure is in unrolling the map, not reading edges. So supply the adjacency list to code and let code do the unrolling.

source: Park, Lee, Lubana, Yang, Okawa, Nishi, Wattenberg, Tanaka (2025) ICLR: In-context learning of representations
finding: Llama-3.1-8B shown random walks on a grid or ring of ordinary words reorganises its internal word geometry to the graph as context grows, with a sudden shift. If the words have a strong prior order (days of the week), the graph structure appears but does not dominate.
numbers: Context lengths about 400 to 1400 tokens in the figures. Task accuracy rises as the Dirichlet energy of the graph falls. Tested square grid, ring and hexagonal grid.
limits: One 8B model and toy graphs. Probe is PCA of mean token states. Prior meanings resist override. Exact accuracies not extracted.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the cognitive-map result: a map forms in context given enough walks. Strong word priors can block it, so give the map in neutral labels.

source: Wu, Mao, Zhang, Xia, Dong, Cui, Wei (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought elicits spatial reasoning
finding: Asking GPT-4 to draw a text grid of the state after each step improved navigation and tiling over plain chain of thought, and beat GPT-4V with images.
numbers: Natural-language navigation: VoT 59.00 vs no-visualisation 35.50 (gain 23.5 points); CoT about 54.00 (p<0.16, not significant). Visual tiling: VoT 63.94 vs CoT 54.15 vs GPT-4V CoT 49.62.
limits: Table text extraction is garbled, so route-planning and next-step cells are not assigned. Small grid worlds; far from perfect on harder items.
agent_relevance: Writing the state as an explicit grid after each step acts as an external map. Supports a code-rendered state view at S2.

source: O'Keefe and Dostrovsky (1971); Hafting et al. (2005); O'Keefe and Nadel (1978): place and grid cell foundation
finding: Place cells in rat hippocampus fire at one location; grid cells in entorhinal cortex fire on a hexagonal lattice. The 1978 book proposed the hippocampus as the cognitive map. Nobel Prize 2014. These are cited as background in CogEval's introduction.
numbers: Not read this session. No figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Background only.
agent_relevance: Anchors the claim that space has a neural map code.

source: Stachenfeld, Botvinick, Gershman (2017) The hippocampus as a predictive map, Nat Neurosci
finding: Proposes place fields encode the successor representation (expected future occupancy), so fields skew toward goals and bend around walls, and grid cells are low-frequency eigenvectors of that matrix. Basis for the 'skew toward goals' phrase in the subfield row.
numbers: Not read: the Nature page redirected to a login. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; summarised only from how Garvert 2017 and Russek 2017 describe it.
agent_relevance: Justifies measuring closeness by predicted reachability.

source: Behrens, Muller, Whittington et al. (2018) What is a cognitive map? Organizing knowledge for flexible behavior, Neuron
finding: Reviews cognitive maps as a representation of relational structure used for inference and generalisation, in space and in abstract spaces.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Definition used by CogEval and by this subfield.

source: Cross-paper contrast: map evidence in brains vs LLMs
finding: Brain studies show a map forms after a few sessions (Garvert one day, Constantinescu 2-4 sessions), yet humans still fail transition changes about half the time. LLM studies show linear maps of fixed facts (Gurnee) and in-context maps in toy graphs (Park), yet planning on novel graphs fails (CogEval policy revaluation 0.21).
numbers: Compiled from lines a05 to a22; no new data.
limits: Studies differ in task, model and year; no head-to-head on one task.
agent_relevance: Representation is not use. The agent should test its map by acting on a changed task, as Tolman did.
